summary: Adds SDC's comments to the discussion of network graphics protocols, with suggestions for supporting data-tablet input devices. It includes the usual disclaimer about ARPA funding and views.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 199 proposes ways to send drawing-tablet input over a network. It distinguishes single points, raw strokes with different timing and data that has already been processed.

subtitle: Proposed message formats for networked data-tablet input.

tldr.problem: Data-tablets can generate large streams of coordinate input with different timing and preprocessing, which a network protocol must represent.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines formats for single-shot, raw asynchronous, raw synchronous and preprocessed tablet data, using initial coordinates and coordinate differences.
tldr.outcome: The RFC contributes suggestions to the network graphics discussion and argues that tablet input should fit alongside non-interactive display graphics.

today: RFC 199 is a network graphics protocol proposal published in July 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Graphics Protocol Approach
sections.content:
The author discusses non-interactive graphics and data-tablet input, rather than fully interactive graphics. The paper recommends starting with simple display generation and adding interactive features as a superset, so added complexity does not burden simpler use.

Tablet input includes X, Y and Z information, where Z indicates whether the stylus is on the writing surface. Sampling can happen once per stroke, on demand or on a clock.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal focuses on sending tablet input and simple graphics. It recommends keeping basic display needs simple and adding interactive features separately.

sections.title: Tablet Input Formats
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four input types: a single-shot point, raw asynchronous data, raw synchronous data and preprocessed data. For raw strokes, it proposes sending an initial coordinate followed by differences from the previous point, with a scale factor for those differences.

The synchronous format also carries sampling-rate information. A preprocessed format can describe filtering and smoothing, include stroke bounds and optionally record counts of rejected points.
sections.plainLanguage: Tablet messages can describe one point or a full pen stroke. A stroke can include raw coordinates, sampling details or information about smoothing and filtering.

sections.title: Preprocessing and Character Display
sections.content:
The paper describes smoothing noisy tablet input and filtering points that fall within a selected window around the last accepted point. It gives an example of an eight-point moving average and describes retaining counts that can help estimate movement speed.

It also discusses flexible character generation. A transmitted character description should identify the code, position, height and width so that generated text can reflect the geometry of the input.
sections.plainLanguage: Tablet software can smooth jitter and remove redundant points before sending a stroke. The message should describe what processing occurred and how displayed characters are sized.
